profile.name: Rinkafadda
profile.tagline: The sixteenth-century Irish long dance uniting all social ranks in public celebration.
profile.insight: In sixteenth-century Ireland, visitors recorded the rinkafadda as an inclusive long dance where entire communities—regardless of social class—formed parallel rows of men and women to join in sequence.
profile.profile: The rinkafadda (Irish: rince fada or rinnce fada, meaning 'long dance') is a historic Irish country or field dance originating in at least the sixteenth century. Danced in two facing rows—one of men and one of women—couples begin at one end of the line, progressively joining until the entire formation dances down to the end and back again. Historical accounts highlight its social inclusiveness and suitability for events of public rejoicing, noting that all social classes participated together. The dance has been linked historically to the Virginia Reel and to the 'fading' mentioned in William Shakespeare's A Winter's Tale.
profile.profile_long:
ORIGINS AND HISTORY
The rinkafadda (Irish: rince fada or rinnce fada, translating literally to 'long dance'), sometimes called the rinka, is an Irish country or field dance that traces its documented existence back to sixteenth-century Ireland. Outside visitors traveling through Ireland during this era recorded detailed descriptions of the dance, marveling at its unique structure and inclusive nature. Historical references frequently associate the rince fada with the evolution of the Virginia Reel as well as the 'fadings', 'The Fading', or the refrain 'With a fading' famously cited by William Shakespeare in Act IV of A Winter's Tale.

HOW IT IS DANCED
The physical structure of the rinkafadda is defined by its longway formation, consisting of a row of men facing an opposing row of women. The performance begins at one end of the set, where the initial couples begin dancing one by one. The movement spreads sequentially down the line until every couple has joined the action. The progression continues down to the opposite end of the line and then reverses direction, carrying the dancers back to their starting places. Specific footwork, body mechanics, tempo, and key hand gestures are not described in sources.

MUSIC AND INSTRUMENTS
As a sixteenth-century Irish country and field dance, the rinkafadda was performed during public outdoors celebrations and gathering events. Details regarding specific musical meter, tempo in beats per minute, rhythmic structures, or instrumental ensembles used to accompany the dance are not described in sources.

COSTUME AND SETTING
The dance was traditionally performed in open fields and countryside settings suitable for gathering large groups of people. Historical accounts specifically note that the dance transcended class boundaries, with members of all social classes taking part together in public spaces during occasions of general rejoicing. Detailed accounts of specific period costumes or garments are not described in sources.

OCCASIONS AND MEANING
The rinkafadda was noted historically for its deep social inclusiveness and its alignment with public rejoicings. Unlike exclusive aristocratic court dances, the rince fada brought whole communities together, allowing people across all social strata to participate in a shared, joyful performance ritual.

NOTABLE FIGURES
No individual historic choreographers, master dancers, or figures are named in historical accounts, though William Shakespeare famously referenced its related form, the 'fading', in his play A Winter's Tale.

REGIONAL VARIANTS
Regional variants or local variations of the rinkafadda across different Irish counties are not described in sources.

LINEAGE
The rinkafadda forms an early core of traditional Irish country dancing. It is historically linked as a direct progenitor or precursor to North American longway set dances like the Virginia Reel, representing a continuous lineage of transatlantic folk dance migration.

sections.origins_and_history: The rinkafadda (Irish: rince fada or rinnce fada, translating to 'long dance') or rinka is an Irish country or field dance dating back to sixteenth-century Ireland. Visitors to Ireland during this era documented its performance. It has been associated historically with the 'Virginia Reel' and the 'fadings', 'The Fading' or 'With a fading' mentioned in Act IV of William Shakespeare's A Winter's Tale.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in a longway set consisting of a row of men facing a row of women. Dancing begins at one end of the line as couples start dancing one by one until all have joined in. The movement travels from one end of the formation to the other and then back again. Specific footwork, body posture, and step counts are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance was performed to music during field gatherings and events of public rejoicing. Specific instruments, rhythm patterns, musical meter, and musical compositions are not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: The rinkafadda was performed outdoors in fields and country settings during events of public rejoicing. Accounts emphasize that all social classes participated in the rince fada together. Period clothing and costume specifics are not described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Noted for its social inclusiveness, the rinkafadda was performed during events of public rejoicing. Its open structure permitted people of all social classes to dance together in shared public celebration.
sections.notable_figures: William Shakespeare associated the related 'fading' in A Winter's Tale. Specific historical dancers or leaders are not described in sources.
sections.regional_variants: Regional variants are not described in sources.

movement_profile.formation_and_space: Two parallel facing rows—one of men and one of women—with couples joining in sequence down the line and back.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Dance That Brought a Divided Ireland Together
episode_brief.logline: Explore how the sixteenth-century Irish long dance crossed social divides and traveled across the Atlantic to influence global folk dance traditions.
beats: Recreate a 16th-century Irish field gathering with two opposing lines of dancers forming in a grassy landscape.
Demonstrate the sequential activation of couples starting at one end of the longway set and moving down the line.
Examine historical visitor accounts detailing how high and low social classes danced together without distinction.
Connect the historic rince fada to Shakespeare's A Winter's Tale and the modern Virginia Reel.

lesson_ladder.goal: Establish line spatial formation and sequential progression.
drills: Form two facing rows of equal length.
Practice sequential entry timing starting from the top couple.

visual_motifs: Parallel facing lines of dancers extending across an outdoor field.
The cascading physical reaction of couples joining the dance one by one.
episode_brief.instructor_persona: An engaging dance historian and Irish traditional culture specialist.
episode_brief.music_cue: Unaccompanied or traditional Irish field tune building in volume as lines join in.
